opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been really excited about in my group. The starting point is a bit of a shift in perspective: normally we think of neural network weights as the end product of training, something you get after running gradient descent for a long time on a dataset. But once you've trained thousands of models, you start to see that the weights themselves form a kind of data modality. We call these collections "model zoos." And if weights are data, then you can ask the same questions you'd ask about images or text: can you learn a representation of them, and can you generate new samples?

So what we did was train what we call hyper-representations. Essentially, we take populations of trained models, tokenize their weights, and learn an autoencoder or a generative model over that weight space. Then you can sample from it and get a completely new set of weights for a network that was never trained with gradient descent, and in many cases those models actually work. They perform well right away, or at least they're a much better starting point than random initialization, so fine-tuning converges faster and often ends up better.

What I find fascinating is that this tells us something about the structure of weight space. It's not just this arbitrary, chaotic high-dimensional thing. There's regularity in it, and the good solutions sit on some kind of manifold you can learn. That opens up a lot: you can generate models conditioned on properties you want, transfer knowledge across architectures, or think about initialization in a data-driven way instead of just using heuristics.

Of course, there are real challenges. Scaling is the big one. Small CNNs are one thing; generating weights for large transformers is much harder, both because of the sheer dimensionality and because of symmetries like permutation invariance that you have to handle carefully. But I think the long-term vision is pretty compelling: instead of always training from scratch, we learn from the collective experience of all the models that have already been trained, and we treat that as a resource in its own right.

r001.rationale: The response says new weights can be sampled from a learned model, but it does not explain that generation uses an inexpensive forward pass or that this makes producing many similar models feasible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about it is that a trained neural network is really just a point in a very high-dimensional weight space, and training is a trajectory through that space. For a long time we've only ever asked: given data, find me that point. The question we started asking in our group in St. Gallen is: can we learn something about the structure of that space itself, and then sample from it directly?

The intuition came from what we called "model zoos." We trained thousands of small networks, same architecture, same task, different seeds and hyperparameters, and then looked at the weights as data. And it turns out they're not random at all. There are clear populations, you can predict a model's test accuracy or even which hyperparameters it was trained with just from looking at its weights. So if weights carry that much structure, it's natural to ask whether you can learn a generative model over them.

The way we approached it, in a line of work we called hyper-representations, is to first learn a compressed latent representation of the weights using something like a transformer-based autoencoder, and then sample in that latent space and decode back into full weight tensors. And those sampled models actually work. Out of the box, without any gradient steps, they land at a reasonable accuracy, and if you fine-tune them for a few epochs they typically reach the performance of models trained from scratch much faster.

Now, I want to be honest about the limitations. The models we've generated are small, think CNNs on MNIST, CIFAR, that scale. Generating the weights of a billion-parameter model directly is a different beast, partly because the weight space is enormous and partly because of symmetries, permutations of neurons that produce functionally identical networks but look completely different as vectors. Handling those symmetries properly is one of the key research problems.

But I think the bigger point is conceptual. We're moving toward a world where we have millions of trained models sitting on Hugging Face, and treating them as a dataset in their own right opens up things like model retrieval, model editing, transfer to new tasks by sampling rather than retraining. So I don't see weight generation as replacing training, I see it as a new way of initializing, adapting, and understanding models that leverages everything we've already learned collectively.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting shift is to treat the weights of a neural network as data. Usually, we train a model on images or text. Here, we learn from a collection of trained models and ask: Can we capture the structure in their weights well enough to generate a new model that actually works?

The challenge is that weights are not just an arbitrary vector. There are dependencies across layers, and two networks can implement the same function while looking quite different in weight space—for example, because you permuted their neurons. So you need a representation that captures something meaningful about the network, rather than just the particular ordering of its parameters.

If you can learn that representation, you can imagine sampling a model, or conditioning generation on a task or a desired property. But the important test is what happens when you put those generated weights into the network and run it. Does it perform the task? Does it generalize? How much additional training does it need? Generating a vector of the right size is easy; generating a useful model is the interesting part.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to stop thinking of a trained model as just one fixed point and start thinking about a distribution over models. If we can learn that distribution in weight space, then we can sample a new set of weights and, in principle, obtain a functioning neural network.

The challenge is that weight space has a lot of structure and symmetry. Two networks can implement the same function while having very different weights—for example, because the neurons are ordered differently. So you cannot simply treat a collection of checkpoints as ordinary vectors and expect a generative model to understand them automatically.

One approach is to learn a compact representation of those weights and then generate within that representation. But the important test is always functional: when you put the generated weights back into the network, does it actually perform the task? Producing weights with plausible statistics is not enough.

I see this as a way to amortize some of the cost of training. You invest in learning from a population of models, and then potentially generate useful models or good initializations much more cheaply. That is a compelling direction, although generating a model that works reliably is a much higher bar than generating something that merely looks like a model in weight space.

r001.rationale: The response says weight generation could produce useful models more cheaply, but it does not explain that an inexpensive forward pass enables producing many similar models.
